newsitem.title: CHINA: Thai offshore FRNs, FRCDs steady, outlook mixed.
newsitem.headline: Thai offshore FRNs, FRCDs steady, outlook mixed.

text.p: Floating rate paper of Thai bank issuers traded in the secondary market were little changed in thin dealings on Thursday, traders said.

Hong Kong traders back at work after an extended holiday said that the floating rate paper market showed little reaction to the Bank of Thailand's announcment on Wednesday that it would float the baht.
In contrast, Thailand's sovereign Yankee bond and other fixed-rate bonds of top Thai borrowers strengthened in New York overnight and maintained a firm tone in Asian trade on Thursday.

Thai floating rate paper, most of which has been issued by banks, has been highly illiquid over the last several months amid investors' efforts to push prices down and holders refusal to sell at much wider spreads.

The Bank of Thailand's move to float the baht, which resulted in a quick and substantial 15-20 percent devaluation of the currency, has been greeted positively by most analysts on views that it paves the way for interest rate cuts and will make Thai exports more competitive.
The baht was trading at 29.00/29.50 per dollar in the offshore market in late trade Thursday compared with 24.25 before the news on Wednesday.
Traders in Hong Kong had mixed views on the outlook for the floating rate paper market.
Some said they expected further widening of spreads.
The de facto devaluation of the baht will raise the cost of servicing dollar debt and could increase Thai banks' foreign exchange losses, depending on how extensively they are hedged, traders said.
That would make Thai bank paper less attractive to investors, they said.
One trader predicted that spreads for top-rated Thai bank paper is likely to widen a few more basis points within a month.
For example, A3-rated Krung Thai Bank's five-year paper, which currently is trading at a spread of around 60 basis points, could widen to 65 basis points, he said.

Traders said there has not been much demand for Thai bank paper generally because of Thailand's financial difficulties this year. Worries about Thai credit quality will continue to dampen demand, they said.
Only slim demand is expected for shorter-dated Thai paper with one to two years remaining until maturity, they said.
Krung Thai Bank's one-year-and-seven-month paper is trading at 50 basis points, giving rise to a rather flat yield curve.
Other traders, however, said they believed Thai paper already has bottomed out.
"I believe Thai paper is on the tightening track," said a trader at a U.S. commercial bank.
"Baht devaluation is a positive move and it can help to boost Thailand's exports," he said.
